cues.text: MIT 8113, Digital Transformation and Innovation.
Study Session 1: The Strategic Role of IT in Digital Transformation.
Chapter one: What transformation actually means.
Let us begin with the central idea.
Digital transformation is a strategic change in how an organisation operates, how it creates and captures value, and how it serves its customers, and it does all of this through digital capabilities.
Notice how wide that definition is.
It is not only about buying software.
It includes changes in people, in processes, in technology, in data, and in business models.
And here is an important qualification: a digital project can contribute to transformation without itself transforming the business.
Installing one new system may be a valuable step, but on its own it does not mean the whole organisation has been transformed.
To make this precise, we need to separate three terms that people often use as if they meant the same thing.
Look at the table that accompanies this lesson.
It has three columns: Term, Meaning, and Nigerian university example.
There are three rows, and we will go through them in order.
The first row is digitisation.
Its meaning is to convert analogue information into digital form.
The Nigerian university example is to scan paper student files.
The paper becomes a digital image, but nothing about how the university works has changed.
The second row is digitalisation.
Its meaning is to improve an existing process using digital tools.
The Nigerian university example is to submit and approve registration online.
The process of registration still exists, but digital tools now carry it out better.
The third row is digital transformation.
Its meaning is to redesign value delivery, the operating model and the capabilities of the organisation.
The Nigerian university example is to deliver flexible online degree programmes with integrated learning, assessment and support.
Here the university is not improving an old process.
It is changing what it offers and how it delivers it.
Let us see the difference in practice.
A scanned form is still a form.
An online form can remove travel and waiting, because a student no longer has to journey to an office and queue.
A redesigned service goes further.
It can remove unnecessary approvals, integrate identity and payments, and provide new learning opportunities.
So the distinction is the scope and the business outcome, not simply the sophistication of the technology.
A very advanced tool used only to scan files is still digitisation.
A modest tool that helps redesign the service can contribute far more.
Why do organisations pursue transformation at all?

The source names several drivers: changing customer expectations, competitive pressure, emerging technologies, cost and efficiency, new revenue opportunities, globalisation, and regulatory requirements.
Context matters too.
In Nigeria, mobile access, payment infrastructure, connectivity, affordability, power reliability and digital literacy all affect which solutions actually create value.
A brilliant digital service that assumes constant electricity or cheap data may fail, however clever it is.
Now let us turn to the second major concept, innovation.
Innovation is the implementation of useful new or improved ideas.
Compare it with two neighbouring words.
Invention creates an idea or a technology; innovation puts it to productive use.
Creativity generates possibilities; innovation requires execution and adoption.
An idea that is never implemented and never adopted is not yet an innovation.
Innovation comes in several types, shown in the second table.
It has three columns: Innovation type, What changes, and Example.
There are six rows.
Row one is product or service innovation.
What changes is the offering.
The example is mobile banking.
Row two is process innovation.
What changes is how work is performed.
The example is automated payment reconciliation.
Row three is business model innovation.
What changes is how value is created, delivered or captured.
The example is subscription streaming.
Row four is incremental innovation.
What changes is a small, continuous improvement.
The example is faster checkout.
Row five is radical innovation.
What changes is that there is substantial novelty.
The example is a fundamentally new technology.
Row six is disruptive innovation.
Here a new approach changes competitive dynamics, often beginning in an underserved market.
The example is new low-cost digital financial services challenging established providers.
One caution about this table.
These categories overlap.
Not every radical invention disrupts a market, and not every process improvement is a business-model change.
A single initiative can belong to more than one category, so treat them as lenses rather than sealed boxes.
Finally, bring the two ideas together.
Digital transformation and innovation reinforce one another.
Technology enables experimentation.
Feedback from that experimentation identifies new opportunities.
And successful innovation becomes part of a new operating model.
That is the cycle to remember: experiment, learn, and then embed what works into the way the organisation runs.
